Rewrite this scene as a literary vignette:
A woman waits alone in a railway station at night. The last train is delayed. She has received a letter she does not want to open.

The station had emptied by degrees, until only the vending machine hummed beside her and the rain tapped lightly against the dark windows. On her lap lay the unopened letter, folded once, its edge softened where her thumb had worried it. The departure board flickered and added another ten minutes. She looked up as though the delay itself required her attention. Somewhere beyond the platform, rails shone under the lamps. The envelope remained closed, patient and exact.

Turn the following description into a short literary passage:
An elderly man closes his small bookshop at the end of the day. He pauses before switching off the final light.

He turned the sign to CLOSED and drew the bolt with the familiar resistance of old metal. The shop settled around him: shelves leaning into shadow, the faint dry scent of paper, a cup left beside the till with a skin of cold tea. His hand reached for the last switch, then stopped. For a moment the narrow aisle remained warm with lamplight. He looked toward the back shelves, where no customer had gone all afternoon, and only then pressed the room into darkness.

Create a literary vignette from this scene:
Two sisters clear breakfast after their children have left for school. They are still annoyed with each other after an argument the night before.

The children had gone noisily, leaving toast crusts, a tipped spoon and one chair pushed too far from the table. The sisters worked without discussing any of it. One stacked bowls more carefully than necessary; the other wiped the same patch of table twice. Outside, a delivery van reversed with patient beeps. When their hands met briefly over the sugar bowl, both withdrew. Neither mentioned the argument. By the time the kitchen was tidy, the silence between them had become the only thing left out.

Render this scene as short literary prose:
A man prepares dinner while waiting for an important phone call. He keeps checking his phone even though it has not rung.

He chopped the onion too finely and noticed only when it had become a wet white heap beneath the knife. The phone lay face-up beside the salt, silent, its black screen catching the kitchen light. Water began to boil, then spat onto the hob. He checked the time again, though only three minutes had passed. By the time the pasta was ready, he had arranged the cutlery for one and moved the phone to the place opposite him, as if expecting it to sit down.

Rewrite this scene as a literary vignette:
A child leaves a favourite toy rabbit on a park bench and only realizes it when the family is already walking home.

They had reached the corner where the park disappeared behind the houses when the child stopped. His hand opened and closed against the empty pocket of his coat. The others were still talking, their steps carrying them forward, before they noticed he was no longer beside them. Back under the plane trees, the bench stood damp from the afternoon mist. On it, the rabbit waited crookedly against the slats, one cloth ear darkened by rain. The child began to run before anyone had answered.

Turn the following description into a short literary passage:
A woman returns to her apartment after being away for several weeks. Nothing has changed, but the place feels unfamiliar.

The key turned reluctantly, though she knew the lock had always done that. Inside, the apartment held its breath. A glass remained upside down beside the sink; a cardigan hung from the chair exactly where she had left it. Dust had gathered lightly along the windowsill, softening the outline of familiar things. She set down her bag but did not remove her coat. The rooms appeared smaller than she remembered, as though they had continued existing without her and had not expected to be interrupted.

Create a literary vignette from this scene:
A student sits outside a professor's office waiting to hear whether she has been accepted for a research placement.

The corridor smelled faintly of coffee and printer paper. She sat beneath a noticeboard crowded with old conference posters, reading the same three titles until their words lost shape. Behind the office door, voices rose and softened, impossible to distinguish. Her notebook rested unopened on her knees. Each time footsteps approached, she straightened, then pretended to study the timetable opposite. At last the handle moved. She looked down at her hands, surprised to find that she had been holding them tightly together.

Render this scene as short literary prose:
A neighbour watches from her window as the family across the street loads the last boxes into a moving van.

By late afternoon the house opposite had begun to show itself: pale rectangles where pictures had hung, bare windows, a hallway visible from the street. She stood behind her curtain with a cup cooling in her hands. The family carried out a final box, then a lamp without its shade. Someone laughed at something she could not hear. When the van doors closed, the sound travelled cleanly across the road. She remained at the window after the engine started, watching an empty driveway come slowly into view.

Rewrite this scene as a literary vignette:
A guest arrives twenty minutes early for a dinner party and waits in the hall while the hosts finish getting ready.

The bell rang while one of the hosts was still barefoot and the other was carrying a stack of plates from the bedroom. Their guest stood in the hall with flowers wrapped in brown paper, apologising for the very punctuality he had chosen. Coats were moved, a chair cleared, a candle lit before its time. From the kitchen came the smell of something beginning to catch. He smiled at every hurried reassurance. For twenty minutes, politeness required all three of them to pretend that nothing had been disturbed.

Turn the following description into a short literary passage:
A woman finds an old cinema ticket in a drawer while looking for a spare key. She cannot immediately remember who she went with.

The ticket lay beneath batteries, receipts and a coil of string, its ink faded to a violet blur at the edges. She had been looking for the spare key and almost threw it aside. Instead she turned it over, though there was nothing written on the back. The date meant something; the title did too. The companion would not come. She stood with the drawer open, listening to the refrigerator start in the next room, and felt the odd embarrassment of having misplaced not an object, but an evening.
